intro.heading: Where price traveled and where price actually closed are two different pieces of information.
intro.body: A wick shows you that price reached an area. A close shows you that price accepted (or rejected) that area. Those are not the same claim, and mixing them up is one of the most common beginner mistakes on a chart. Price can wick well above a level and still close back below it — that's not the same as price closing above the level. This distinction matters far beyond this lesson: later in the Academy, an entire entry model is built around the rule that a candle has to close past a level, not just poke a wick through it.
intro.dayliNote: "I don't care about the wick. I need the candle to close through the level. Say that back to yourself every time you're tempted to react to a wick." — Dayli Scott

chart.heading: Wick vs close, side by side
chart.prompt: A candle wicks above a key high but closes back below it. See what the wick did NOT hold.

config.caption: Tap "Show the rejection" to see what the wick did not hold

tapCards.prompt: A candle wicks above a key high but closes back below it. Has that level been broken?

options.label: No — it wicked through but didn't close through
options.feedback: Right — a wick is a visit, not a break.

options.label: Yes — price touched above it
options.feedback: Touching a level isn't the same claim as closing past it.

tapCards.prompt: Later, a candle both wicks above that same high AND closes above it. What's different this time?

options.label: This time price actually accepted above the level — a real close-based break
options.feedback: Right — a close through the level is a genuinely different claim than a wick through it.

options.label: Nothing's different — wick or close, both count the same
options.feedback: They don't count the same — only the close shows acceptance.

tapCards.prompt: Later in the Academy, an entire entry model requires a candle to close past a level before anything else matters. Why does the close matter that much?

options.label: Because a close is the only thing that shows price genuinely accepted that area
options.feedback: Exactly — that's the whole reason close-based confirmation becomes the rule.

options.label: Because wicks are too hard to see on a chart
options.feedback: It's not about visibility — it's about what a close actually proves.

quiz.question: Price takes a previous high with a wick but closes back below it. Has bullish structure necessarily been confirmed?
options: No — a wick shows price reached the level, but only a close through it shows acceptance
Yes — any candle touching above the high confirms the break
It depends only on the candle's color, not where it closed
quiz.explanation: Reaching a level and accepting past it are two different claims.

quiz.question: A trader gets excited every time she sees a wick poke through a key level, treating it as confirmation. What is she misunderstanding?
options: She's treating a wick (where price traveled) as if it were a close (where price accepted)
She should be looking at volume instead
quiz.explanation: Confirmation should come from a close past the level, not a wick poking through it.

quiz.question: A wick tells you where price ___. A close tells you where price accepted.
quiz.explanation: The wick is just the extreme reached — not proof of acceptance.
